slides.title: Brand
slides.body: Welcome!
slides.notes: The opening mark. Content rule 21 keeps "Welcome to today's session" for the next frame, so this one says something else.
slides.label: Brand

slides.title: Welcome
slides.notes: The session name, in minimal mode: the kicker and the title, nothing else.
slides.label: Welcome

slides.title: What We Will Cover
slides.notes: The TR's own agenda, all five items, split at the colon it writes. These exact strings come back on the Key Takeaways frame (content rule 20).
slides.label: Agenda

slides.title: Section: Cloud Computing Basics
slides.notes: TR section 1. The subtitle is the agenda's own sub for this section.
slides.label: Section divider

slides.title: Why Cloud Emerged
slides.body:
Cloud Computing Overview
Traditional IT ties hardware purchases to guesses about future demand, locking capital years before the load actually arrives.
On-premise IT
organisation buys, installs, maintains hardware
Cloud IT
computing rented as a metered service
Shift driven by cost, scale and speed pressures
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Split-screen diagram: left a server room with racks and IT staff, right a laptop reaching a cloud icon over the network." The panels carry the TR's first two bullets as their own bodies and the third is the caption, so the same three strings are not on the frame twice. TR speaker notes: "Set up the capacity-planning problem before naming cloud computing as the fix. Interviewers often open this topic by asking what problem cloud computing actually solves."
slides.label: Why cloud emerged

slides.title: NIST Formal View
slides.body:
Cloud Computing Defined
Five essential characteristics govern shared resource access
Three service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
Four deployment models: public, private, hybrid, community
AWS Management Console exposes this self-service resource catalog
NIST Definition
The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) defines cloud computing as a model for enabling anywhere, convenient, on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources (networks, servers, storage, applications, and services) that can be rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort or service provider interaction.
slides.notes: The TR's Content paragraph for this slide is the NIST definition, 55 words of it. It is set as the definition callout rather than as a lead: six lines of 22px lead type pushes the rest of the slide off the canvas, and this is the one sentence in the session the room is most likely to be asked to reproduce. TR speaker notes: "Name NIST SP 800-145 as the source so the definition is quoted correctly. This exact definition is a frequent interview question, so state it precisely."
slides.label: NIST formal view

slides.title: NIST Formal View
slides.body:
Cloud Computing Defined
NIST Definition
Essential Characteristics
five of them
Service Models
IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
Deployment Models
public, private, hybrid, community
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Central box labelled 'NIST Definition' branching into three labelled boxes: Essential Characteristics, Service Models, Deployment Models." It gets its own frame because it needs the full width: squeezed into a side column beside the definition and four bullets, its third label ran off the bottom of the canvas and into the footer mark, which is what `qa.mjs` and `align-check.mjs` both reported. Same kicker and title as the frame before it, so `continuity.ts` holds the header still: one heading, a second exhibit. Only the characteristics are opened in this session; the service and deployment models are the next session, so name them and move on (content rule 4).
slides.label: NIST: three branches

slides.title: Analogy: a furnished apartment
slides.body:
Cloud Computing Defined
A furnished apartment
Cloud computing
Move in, do not build
slides.notes: TR analogy, verbatim: "Renting a furnished apartment instead of constructing a house gives instant living space without owning bricks or cement — just as cloud computing gives access to configurable computing resources on demand without owning the underlying infrastructure." Say it; the frame draws it. The three mapping rows are what the room can check, so walk them left to right.
slides.label: Analogy: a furnished apartment

slides.title: Ownership and Delivery
slides.body:
On-Premise vs Cloud
On-premise IT keeps hardware, software and staff inside the organisation; cloud shifts ownership and operation to a provider, delivered over the network.
A locked data centre
Reachable from anywhere over the internet
Aspect
On-Premise IT
Cloud
Ownership
Organisation owns hardware
Provider owns infrastructure
Cost model
Capital expenditure (CapEx)
Operating expenditure (OpEx)
Provisioning time
Weeks to months
Minutes
Scaling
Manual hardware upgrade
On-demand, software-driven
Maintenance
In-house IT team
Provider-managed
slides.notes: Both of the TR's visuals are here: "Two-panel diagram: left a locked data-centre building, right a cloud icon reachable from anywhere over the internet", above the five-row table. The panels are in label-only mode, because their job on this frame is to say what is being compared before the table compares it. Five rows, values exactly as the TR sets them. TR speaker notes: "Stress the CapEx-to-OpEx shift as the single biggest contrast for interviews. Ask learners to map each row to a real purchase decision they know."
slides.label: On-premise vs cloud

slides.title: Cloud Computing Architecture
slides.body: On-Premise vs Cloud
slides.notes: THE TR DOC'S OWN DIAGRAM, REDRAWN. It is embedded in the document between the on-premise/cloud table and that slide's Visual Guidance line, and both builds before this one missed it because the Drive connector's text representation of a Google Doc drops embedded images silently: nothing in the text said an image was there. It only appeared on an export to HTML. Walk the numbers: 1 is the front end, 9 is the internet between the halves, and 2 to 6 are the back-end layers with management and security running down both sides. Nothing on it is opened here; these layers are what the rest of the course builds on. IT IS NOT THE SOURCE PNG. The designer's deck embeds that same image byte for byte (md5 73ee77...), and the instruction was to take the reference and draw our own, so `CloudArchitecture` redraws it in the deck's blue at the deck's type sizes, animating top down. Every label and every number is the source's.
slides.label: Cloud computing architecture

slides.title: Cost Scale Speed
slides.body:
Adoption Drivers
Three pressures push organisations toward cloud: unpredictable cost of owning hardware, difficulty scaling for sudden demand, and slow speed of provisioning new infrastructure.
Cost
converts CapEx to pay-per-use OpEx, cuts idle capacity
Scale
resources added or removed as demand shifts
Speed
servers provisioned in minutes, not procurement cycles
Cloud Adoption
Reflected in tools like AWS Cost Explorer, Pricing Calculator
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Three icons in a row — a rupee coin, an elastic band, a stopwatch — each labelled cost, scale, speed, feeding one arrow marked 'Cloud Adoption'." The three tiles carry the TR's first three bullets verbatim and the fourth is the caption. TR speaker notes: "Tie each driver to a concrete AWS tool so the point feels practical, not abstract. Interviewers often ask learners to justify a cloud migration using exactly these three drivers."
slides.label: Adoption drivers

slides.title: Section: History & Evolution
slides.notes: TR section 2.
slides.label: Section divider

slides.title: From Mainframes To Cloud
slides.body:
Four Eras Of Computing
Cloud computing did not appear overnight; it inherited ideas from four earlier eras, each solving the resource-sharing problem of its own time.
1960s-70s
mainframes & time-sharing
1980s-2000s
client-server & x86 virtualization
1990s-2000s
grid & utility computing
2006 onward
the public cloud era
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Horizontal timeline strip with four labelled eras and simple icons: mainframe terminal, PC-plus-server, linked grid nodes, cloud symbol." The stops ARE the TR's four bullets, split at the colon the TR writes, so the four era strings appear once rather than twice. TR speaker notes: "Frame this as the roadmap for the section before going era by era. Exam angle: each era is often asked as 'what did X contribute to cloud computing'."
slides.label: Four eras of computing

slides.title: One Machine Many Users
slides.body:
Mainframes & Time-Sharing
Early mainframes were too costly for one user alone, so time-sharing let many users access the same machine at once.
Mainframes: centralised, costly machines run by dedicated operators
Batch processing: jobs queued and run without interaction
Time-sharing (1960s): CPU scheduled across simultaneous terminal users
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Mainframe box with several terminal lines converging on it, a small clock icon marking scheduled turns." The lines point INWARD, which is why this is not `RadialSpread`: the claim is four terminals queueing for one machine, not one machine reaching four terminals. The fifth bullet's em dash became a colon (content rule 1). TR speaker notes: "Time-sharing is the first appearance of the resource-multiplexing idea cloud scales up massively. Exam angle: contrast queued batch jobs against interactive time-sharing."
slides.label: Mainframes and time-sharing

slides.title: One Machine Many Users
slides.body:
Mainframes & Time-Sharing
Each user experienced an illusion of a private computer
IBM's CP-40/CP-67 (1960s) pioneered mainframe virtualization: the earliest form of the concept
Terminal
Mainframe
CPU scheduled across simultaneous terminal users
scheduled turns
slides.notes: The two bullets the converging-terminals figure does not illustrate: what each user experienced, and the IBM machines that got there first. They are on their own frame because this slide measured 459 characters of lead-plus-bullets against a ~420 comfort ceiling, and five two-line bullets beside a figure is the densest thing in the deck.
slides.label: Mainframes and time-sharing, continued

slides.title: Analogy: a library reading room
slides.body:
Mainframes & Time-Sharing
A library reading room
Time-sharing
Everyone gets a scheduled turn
slides.notes: TR analogy, verbatim: "A library reading room with one shared encyclopedia set, where each reader gets a scheduled turn at the desk — just as time-sharing gave every terminal user a scheduled turn on one mainframe." The third mapping row is the one worth pressing: the reason to share was never fairness, it was that the machine was too expensive to leave idle.
slides.label: Analogy: a library reading room

slides.title: Hardware Gets Abstracted
slides.body:
Client-Server & Virtualization
Personal computers and networks split work into client requests and dedicated servers; virtualization then lets one physical server run several independent virtual machines.
1980s-90s: client-server split desktop and network-server roles
Commodity x86 virtualization (late 1990s onward, e.g. VMware): a hypervisor partitions one server
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Diagram: physical server box, hypervisor layer above it, three VM boxes each with its own OS icon on top." `LayerStack` in the kit stacks full-width bands, which would draw the three VMs as layers OF each other; the side-by-side row is the point, because it is what isolation looks like. TR speaker notes: "Virtualization is the direct technical ancestor of cloud multi-tenancy taught later in this session. Interview angle: explain how a hypervisor isolates VMs sharing one host."
slides.label: Client-server and virtualization

slides.title: Hardware Gets Abstracted
slides.body:
Client-Server & Virtualization
Each virtual machine runs its own OS, isolated from others
Decouples software from physical hardware, enabling resource pooling
VM
its own OS
VM
its own OS
VM
its own OS
Hypervisor
One physical server
slides.notes: What the hypervisor buys, once it has partitioned the server: isolation per virtual machine, and hardware the software no longer depends on. Split off because the frame before it measured 459 characters.
slides.label: Client-server and virtualization, continued

slides.title: Analogy: a subdivided plot
slides.body:
Client-Server & Virtualization
One plot, locked apartments
Virtual machines
One space, divided and locked
slides.notes: TR analogy, verbatim: "One large plot subdivided into separate, locked apartments by a building's structure — just as a hypervisor partitions one physical server into isolated virtual machines, each unaware of its neighbours." The middle row is the one that matters: the structure does the dividing, and a tenant cannot undo it from inside their own flat.
slides.label: Analogy: a subdivided plot

slides.title: Pooling And Metering Power
slides.body:
Grid & Utility Computing
Grid computing pooled processing power across many organisations for one large task, while utility computing proposed billing that powers the way electricity is billed.
Grid computing: idle CPUs across institutions combined for shared jobs
Example: distributed scientific projects pooling volunteer processing power
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Diagram: multiple institution icons linked into one central grid; a separate metering gauge icon beside it for billing." The gauge sits beside the hub rather than inside it, because the TR names it as a separate thing: what it measures is the sharing, not the machines. TR speaker notes: "Grid pioneered pooling distributed compute; utility pioneered pay-per-use billing, both feeding directly into cloud. Interview angle: distinguish grid (pooled computation) from cloud (pooled plus on-demand self-service)."
slides.label: Grid and utility computing

slides.title: Pooling And Metering Power
slides.body:
Grid & Utility Computing
Utility computing: pay only for capacity consumed, not owned
Both separate consumption from ownership of hardware, ahead of cloud
Institution
One grid
Idle CPUs combined for shared jobs
metered billing
slides.notes: The utility half of the pair. Grid pooled the capacity; utility billed for what was consumed, and the two together are what cloud inherited. Split off because the frame before it measured 441 characters.
slides.label: Grid and utility computing, continued

slides.title: Analogy: a shared truck fleet
slides.body:
Grid & Utility Computing
One shipping company's trucks
Grid and utility computing
Pool the load, pay your share
slides.notes: TR analogy, verbatim: "Several small businesses sharing one shipping company's trucks, pooling partial loads and paying only for the weight each one ships — just as grid computing pools spare processing power and utility computing bills only for capacity consumed." Two ideas in one picture, and they are the two eras: the fleet is grid computing, paying by weight is utility computing.
slides.label: Analogy: a shared truck fleet

slides.title: 2006 Onward Milestones
slides.body:
Public Cloud Emerges
The public cloud era began when providers started selling the pooled, virtualized, metered resources of earlier eras directly over the internet, on demand.
2006
Amazon Web Services launches S3 storage, then EC2 compute
2008
Google App Engine offers a managed application platform
2010
Microsoft launches Windows Azure commercially
By the 2010s
public cloud becomes the default for new IT
Adoption
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Timeline strip from 2006 to 2010s with provider logos placed at their launch years and a rising adoption curve beneath." The four stops are the TR's own four milestone lines, which it writes as three plain lines and one bullet. The marks come from `slide-kit/assets/companies/` (content rule 13), each the vendor's own, unrecoloured. TR speaker notes: "AWS's 2006 launch is the commonly cited start of the modern public cloud industry. Exam angle: know that S3 preceded EC2 within that same year."
slides.label: Public cloud emerges

slides.title: Eras And Their Legacy
slides.body:
Evolution At A Glance
Each era solved a resource problem that cloud computing still answers, from shared access on one machine to metered, on-demand delivery over the internet.
1960s-70s
1980s-2000s
1990s-2000s
2006 onward
Era
Period
Core Idea
Cloud Legacy
Mainframes & Time-sharing
1960s-70s
Many users share one machine
Shared-access roots
Client-Server & Virtualization
1980s-2000s
Hardware abstracted into virtual machines
Resource pooling
Grid & Utility Computing
1990s-2000s
Pooled capacity, pay-per-use billing
Metered service model
Public Cloud
2006 onward
On-demand delivery over internet
Today's cloud platforms
slides.notes: Both of the TR's visuals: "Full four-row table on screen with a slim timeline ribbon above it repeating the four eras in sequence." The ribbon carries the periods only; the era names are in the table's first column directly beneath it, and printing them twice on one frame is the redundancy a ribbon is trying to avoid. Values exactly as the TR sets them. TR speaker notes: "This table is a frequent interview question on cloud history. Ask learners to match each precursor model to the cloud characteristic it most resembles."
slides.label: Evolution at a glance

slides.title: Quiz time
slides.notes: Placed here on instruction: the quiz goes immediately after the second topic. Everything from here on assumes the room can already read mainframe, time-sharing, hypervisor and grid, so a misunderstanding caught here does not compound through the three sections that follow. This is the For Loop session's own frame, byte for byte. Open the quiz on the portal, everyone answers alone, then go through the answers together.
slides.label: Quiz time

slides.title: Section: Essential Characteristics - I
slides.notes: TR section 3.
slides.label: Section divider

slides.title: Five NIST Traits
slides.body:
Essential Characteristics
NIST formally defines cloud computing through five essential characteristics, the standard checklist that distinguishes cloud from traditional IT.
slides.notes: REDRAWN FROM THE TR DOC'S OWN DIAGRAM, and it is exactly what its Visual Guidance line asks for: "five-box diagram, each box labelled with one NIST characteristic name, arranged around a central 'Cloud' icon". The source image is embedded in the document and was invisible to the Drive connector's text read, which is why the first two builds drew a substitute for it; the designer's deck then turned out to embed the very same PNG (md5 b7ddbc...). This is the same composition in the deck's own palette and type, which is what was asked for: take the reference, do not ship the image. Name the five going round the ring; the frame after this one glosses them. TR speaker notes: "The five traits together form the complete NIST definition of cloud computing."
slides.label: Five NIST traits

slides.title: Five NIST traits, glossed
slides.body:
Essential Characteristics
On-demand self-service: provisioning without human intervention
Broad network access: reachable over standard protocols
Resource pooling: shared infrastructure across multiple tenants
Rapid elasticity: capacity scales automatically with demand
Measured service: usage metered and billed per consumption
slides.notes: The TR's own five bullets, each split at the colon it writes: the name, then what it means. They get their own frame because five two-line bullets beside the diagram ran off the bottom of the canvas, and because the picture and the gloss are two beats rather than one. Same kicker and title as the diagram before them, so `continuity.ts` holds the header still. This is the one place in the deck that introduces five terms at once, because it is the TR's overview frame and the three slides after it open them one at a time.
slides.label: Five NIST traits, glossed

slides.title: No Human Intervention
slides.body:
On-Demand Self-Service
On-demand self-service lets a customer provision computing resources automatically, without requiring a phone call or ticket to the provider's staff.
Customer requests via console, CLI or API
Contrasts with traditional IT: weeks-long procurement tickets
AWS: EC2 'Launch Instance' or CLI run-instances call
Console
CLI
API
Weeks-long procurement ticket
Resources provisioned
without human intervention
slides.notes: TR visual guidance asked for a "screenshot-style mockup: AWS console 'Launch Instance' button highlighted, arrow showing instant provisioning with no approval step in between". A reconstructed screenshot is exactly what content rules 11 and 30 forbid, and no real capture of Launch Instance exists in the asset library or any course's captures, so this draws the mechanism and the plan carries the capture as outstanding work. The struck-through ticket is the figure's argument: what the slide asserts is the ABSENCE of a step, and an absence drawn as a gap is invisible. TR speaker notes: "Contrast this with traditional data-centre provisioning, which needed weeks of approval tickets."
slides.label: On-demand self-service

slides.title: Analogy: an ATM
slides.body:
On-Demand Self-Service
An ATM
On-demand self-service
Nobody to ask first
slides.notes: TR analogy, verbatim: "An ATM lets a customer withdraw cash any time, without a bank clerk approving each transaction — just as on-demand self-service lets a customer provision cloud resources instantly without provider staff involvement." The middle row is the characteristic: what makes it self-service is the approval step that is not there.
slides.label: Analogy: an ATM

slides.title: Ubiquitous Standard Access
slides.body:
Broad Network Access
Broad network access means cloud resources are reachable over standard network protocols from heterogeneous client devices, laptops, phones or thin clients alike.
AWS API
Laptop
HTTPS/API
Mobile app
HTTPS/API
Browser console
HTTPS/API
CLI
HTTPS/API
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Diagram: single AWS icon at centre, arrows fanning out to laptop, phone, browser and CLI-terminal icons, each arrow labelled 'HTTPS/API'." `RadialSpread` is the right kit figure here and the wrong one two sections back: this claim really does point outward, one API reached from four kinds of client. The mark is the vendor's own from `slide-kitdata:image/png;base64,` (content rules 12 and 13). TR speaker notes: "This leans on already-known HTTP and client-server concepts, now applied to cloud access. A private, LAN-only application lacks this same universal reachability."
slides.label: Broad network access

slides.title: Shared Infrastructure Model
slides.body:
Pooling And Multi-Tenancy
Resource pooling means provider infrastructure is shared across customers, with capacity assigned dynamically rather than dedicated per customer.
Multi-tenancy: multiple customers share same physical hardware
Hypervisor: virtualization software splitting one server into isolated tenants
Location independence: customer unaware of physical resource
AWS: EC2 hosts run multiple tenants via shared hypervisor
Tenant A
Tenant B
Tenant C
Hypervisor
Shared physical hardware
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Diagram: one physical server icon with a hypervisor layer, three tenant boxes (A, B, C) each drawing a slice dynamically from the shared pool." Same figure as the virtualization slide with the top row relabelled, which is the point: the TR is saying multi-tenancy IS that mechanism applied to customers. TR speaker notes: "Emphasise that hypervisor-enforced isolation is what keeps tenant data separate on shared hardware."
slides.label: Pooling and multi-tenancy

slides.title: Analogy: a hostel mess kitchen
slides.body:
Pooling And Multi-Tenancy
A hostel mess kitchen
Resource pooling
One stock, portions on demand
slides.notes: TR analogy, verbatim: "A hostel mess kitchen serves many students from one shared stock of vessels, portioning food on demand instead of giving each student a dedicated stove — exactly as resource pooling shares infrastructure dynamically across tenants." The last row is the one to press: pooling is defined by what is NOT dedicated.
slides.label: Analogy: a hostel mess kitchen

slides.title: Section: Essential Characteristics - II
slides.notes: TR section 4.
slides.label: Section divider

slides.title: Elasticity Scalability Metering
slides.body:
Three Characteristics Overview
Cloud platforms must absorb changing demand and charge only for what gets used. Three characteristics make that possible: rapid elasticity, scalability, and measured service.
Rapid elasticity
automatic scale-out and scale-in with demand
Scalability
capacity to grow, vertically or horizontally
Measured service
usage tracked and billed per resource consumed
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Three-panel diagram: an elastic demand curve with scaling arrows in and out, beside a meter icon feeding a billing screen." The three panels carry the TR's three bullets, split at the colon it writes; the curve and the meter are drawn in full on the two slides that follow, where each is the slide's own subject. `CardGrid` click-gates its cards, so this is a three-beat build: name each characteristic as it lands. TR speaker notes: "Distinguish elasticity's automatic, reversible scaling from scalability's broader capacity question before tracing a live example."
slides.label: Three characteristics overview

slides.title: Auto-Scaling Mechanism
slides.body:
Rapid Elasticity
Rapid elasticity is the cloud's ability to provision and release resources - in most cases automatically, almost instantly, as demand rises or falls.
Triggered by real-time metrics, such as CloudWatch alarms
Auto Scaling Groups add or remove instances within minutes
Scales in both directions: out under load, in after
Cost: extra capacity billed only while it actually runs
Demand
Instance count
CloudWatch alarm triggers the Auto Scaling Group
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Timeline graph showing traffic spike with instance-count line rising then falling back to baseline, an Auto Scaling Group icon triggering the change." Demand is a smooth curve and instance count is a STEP line, deliberately: a server either exists or does not, and drawing the count smoothly would assert that 2.4 instances is a thing. The lead keeps the TR's own hyphen; content rule 1 bans the spaced EM dash, which this is not. TR speaker notes: "Elasticity is automatic and reversible, unlike a one-time capacity upgrade."
slides.label: Rapid elasticity

slides.title: Analogy: a rubber band
slides.body:
Rapid Elasticity
A rubber band
Rapid elasticity
Stretch, then spring back
slides.notes: TR analogy, verbatim: "A rubber band stretches under load and springs back once released — just as auto-scaled capacity expands during a spike and contracts once demand fades." The second and third rows are the whole distinction from scalability, which is coming next: a band that stretched and stayed stretched would not be elastic.
slides.label: Analogy: a rubber band

slides.title: Traffic Spike Traced
slides.body:
Elasticity Vs Scalability
During a demand surge, elasticity reacts automatically to the moment; scalability asks whether the underlying architecture can absorb growth at all.
Elasticity
Instance count
Scalability
Instance size
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Side-by-side bar chart: instance count over time showing elasticity's spike-and-return versus a step-change resize for scalability." Both are step lines, because both are whole-number changes, and both use the SAME y scale so the shapes can be compared: one goes up and comes back, one goes up and stays. That contrast is the slide. The table that states it in words is the next frame.
slides.label: Elasticity vs scalability charts

slides.title: Traffic Spike Traced
slides.body:
Elasticity Vs Scalability
Aspect
Elasticity
Scalability
Trigger
Real-time demand (CloudWatch alarm)
Planned capacity growth
Timescale
Minutes, fully automatic
Hours to days, manual or automated
Direction
Scales out and back in
Mostly one-directional growth
Worked case
2→10 instances in ~3 min, back to 2
m5.large resized to m5.4xlarge in advance
slides.notes: Four rows, values exactly as the TR sets them, arrows included. The TR writes the worked case as `2→10 instances in \~3 min`; the backslash is a Google Docs escape, not content, so the cell reads `2→10 instances in ~3 min`. Same kicker and title as the chart frame before it, deliberately: `continuity.ts` holds the header still, so the room reads one heading with a second exhibit under it. TR speaker notes: "Trace the same flash-sale scenario for both terms so the contrast stays concrete. The trigger and timescale columns are the quick answer."
slides.label: Elasticity vs scalability table

slides.title: Pay-Per-Use Metering
slides.body:
Measured Service
Measured service means cloud providers automatically monitor, meter and report resource usage, so bills map directly to actual consumption.
Metrics tracked: compute-seconds, storage-GB, data transfer, API calls
CloudWatch collects usage; Billing and Cost Explorer compute charges
Granular units: EC2 per-second, S3 per-GB-month, Lambda per-request
No usage recorded means no charge: true pay-per-use pricing
CloudWatch

slides.title: CapEx To OpEx
slides.body:
Cost Model Shift
On-premise IT demands large upfront capital expenditure on hardware before any workload runs. Cloud shifts most of that spend to metered operating expenditure, billed for resources as they're consumed.
No upfront hardware purchase or depreciation schedule
Spend scales largely with actual resource usage (committed-use options like Reserved Instances trade some flexibility for lower rates)
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Two bars side by side: a tall one-time CapEx spike versus a flat recurring OpEx line over time." Both panels share ONE ceiling, which is the only reason the figure means anything: scaled independently they would draw the same height and say the opposite of the slide. The bars are a shape, not a claim about anyone's spend, and carry no rupee figures. TR speaker notes: "The shift is financial, not technical — the underlying compute still runs somewhere."
slides.label: Cost model shift

slides.title: Scale Reach Speed
slides.body:
Growth And Speed Benefits
Elasticity, global reach and speed to market convert cloud's technical flexibility into concrete business value: faster launches, worldwide presence and lower idle spend.
Elasticity: autoscaling matches spend to real-time load
Global reach: new AWS Region live in minutes
Speed to market: idea to production in days
Real-world: AWS Auto Scaling groups, Global Infrastructure Region map
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "World map with AWS Region markers lighting up one after another, alongside a rising-then-falling autoscaling curve." This is the one figure in the deck that is a REAL capture rather than a drawing, reused from the Deployment course and re-copied through `cloud_computing_course/workflow/captures/` (content rule 13). Re-capture it if AWS redraws the page. The autoscaling curve is drawn in full on the elasticity slide, where it is the subject, so it is not repeated here. TR speaker notes: "Tie the benefit back to the underlying elasticity mechanism rather than the marketing phrase alone."
slides.label: Growth and speed benefits

slides.title: Switching Cost Risk
slides.body:
Vendor Lock-In
Deep reliance on one provider's proprietary APIs, data formats or managed services makes moving a workload elsewhere slow, risky and expensive.
Proprietary services (Lambda triggers, DynamoDB APIs) resist portability
Data egress fees add direct exit cost
Team skill-set built around one provider's tools
Mitigation: multi-cloud design, open standards, Infrastructure as Code
One provider
Your application
Lambda triggers
DynamoDB APIs
Data egress fees
Other providers
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "Icon of an application boxed inside one provider's logo, with a locked padlock on the arrow pointing toward other providers." The nesting is the argument: lock-in is not "the app talks to one provider", it is that the app is built out of that provider's parts, so the boundary runs around it. The destination box is drawn at full strength and not faded, because content rule 4 forbids greying out a real option. TR speaker notes: "Lock-in is a design-time risk that compounds with every proprietary service adopted, not a one-time migration cost."
slides.label: Vendor lock-in

slides.title: Analogy: fitted cupboards
slides.body:
Vendor Lock-In
A landlord's fitted cupboards
Vendor lock-in
Fitted things do not move
slides.notes: TR analogy, verbatim: "A rented apartment fitted with the landlord's custom cupboards works only in that apartment — just as an application built entirely on one cloud's proprietary APIs runs only on that cloud." The analogy is about DESIGN choices, not about the rental: every cupboard was a decision someone made, which is the point of the mitigation bullet on the frame before this one.
slides.label: Analogy: fitted cupboards

slides.title: Unplanned Billing Risk
slides.body:
Cost Overruns
Pay-per-use billing grows silently with usage, unlike a fixed on-premise budget; unmonitored or misconfigured resources can turn into a large, unexpected bill.
Idle or forgotten resources keep billing after use
Misconfigured autoscaling can multiply costs unexpectedly
Data transfer and API charges accumulate unnoticed
AWS Budgets and Cost Anomaly Detection flag abnormal spend
Monthly bill
An unmonitored resource kept billing
slides.notes: TR visual guidance: "A steadily climbing bill graph with a red spike where an unmonitored resource kept running." Same chart component as the elasticity slide, in its bill variant: the shape is the whole content, so it is derived from values rather than hand-drawn. No amount is shown, because no amount is known. TR speaker notes: "Stress that cost overruns are an operational discipline problem, not a pricing flaw."
slides.label: Cost overruns

slides.title: Distance And Law Limits
slides.body:
Latency And Residency
Physical distance to the nearest AWS Region adds network delay, and certain data must legally remain within national borders regardless of which Region is closest.
Mitigation: nearest Region or a CDN edge location
Data residency: laws such as GDPR require in-country storage
AWS Region selection at creation enforces residency choice

It is NOT drawn as a world map: a hand-drawn coastline at this size carries no real geography and content rule 8 wants the slide's own concept, not the topic in general. The real AWS Region map is used three slides back, as a genuine capture. Every element the TR lists is here; only the coastline is not, and the coastline was never the teaching. The user and the near Region sit INSIDE one dashed enclosure, because that is what the law says. TR speaker notes: "Distinguish latency as a performance concern from data residency as a legal constraint."
